items.followUp: Define melting point and state one factor that affects it.

rubric.why: A correct definition must identify the condition at boiling.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point as the temperature at which a liquid’s vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining condition and temperature.

rubric.why: Boiling point changes with external pressure.
rubric.description: States that increasing external pressure raises the boiling point (and decreasing it lowers the boiling point).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct pressure trend.

rubric.why: Stronger attractions between molecules require more energy to overcome.
rubric.description: Relates stronger intermolecular forces to a higher boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct relationship.

rubric.why: Dissolved non-volatile impurities generally elevate a liquid’s boiling point.
rubric.description: States that non-volatile impurities raise the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of impurities.

modelAnswer: The boiling point of a liquid is the temperature at which its vapour pressure becomes equal to the atmospheric pressure.
Increasing external pressure raises the boiling point; decreasing pressure lowers it.
Liquids with stronger intermolecular forces have higher boiling points.
Dissolved non-volatile impurities generally raise the boiling point.

items.followUp: Write four properties of a true solution.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles are defined by their intermediate size range.
rubric.description: Gives the colloidal particle-size range as about 1–1000 nm.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct range.

rubric.why: A colloid is heterogeneous even though it may appear homogeneous.
rubric.description: Identifies a colloid as a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this characteristic.

rubric.why: Scattering light is a characteristic optical property of colloids.
rubric.description: States that colloids show the Tyndall effect or scatter light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either expression of light scattering.

rubric.why: Colloidal particles remain dispersed and exhibit characteristic movement.
rubric.description: States that particles do not settle on standing, or that they show Brownian motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either valid characteristic.

modelAnswer: A colloid is a heterogeneous mixture with particle sizes of about 1–1000 nm.
Colloidal particles scatter light, showing the Tyndall effect.
The particles do not settle on standing.

rubric.why: The named forms must be different isotopes of the same element.
rubric.description: Gives two different isotopes of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any correct pair of hydrogen isotopes.

rubric.why: These are two commonly given isotopes of chlorine.
rubric.description: Gives chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 as isotopes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct chlorine isotope pair.

modelAnswer: Two examples are the isotopes of hydrogen: protium (¹H), deuterium (²H) and tritium (³H).
Another example is chlorine-35 (³⁵Cl) and chlorine-37 (³⁷Cl).

items.followUp: State one achievement and one limitation of Rutherford’s atomic model.

rubric.why: The model could not account for why orbiting electrons do not lose energy and fall into the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model failed to explain the stability of the atom.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the stability defect.

rubric.why: The model did not explain the observed discrete spectral lines of atoms.
rubric.description: States that Rutherford’s model failed to explain atomic line spectra.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the spectral defect.

modelAnswer: Rutherford’s model could not explain the stability of the atom: revolving electrons should lose energy and fall into the nucleus.
It also could not explain the line spectra of atoms.

items.followUp: Describe how atomic radius changes across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: This is the general periodic trend in ionization energy across a period.
rubric.description: States that ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct across-period trend.

rubric.why: This is the general periodic trend in ionization energy down a group.
rubric.description: States that ionization energy generally decreases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct down-group trend.

modelAnswer: Ionization energy generally increases from left to right across a period.
Ionization energy generally decreases down a group.

items.followUp: What is meant by shielding effect in an atom?

rubric.why: Effective nuclear charge is the net attraction from the nucleus experienced by an electron.
rubric.description: Identifies effective nuclear charge as the net positive charge or attraction experienced by an electron.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the idea of a net nuclear charge acting on an electron.

rubric.why: The definition distinguishes the nuclear charge experienced by an outer electron from the full nuclear charge.
rubric.description: Mentions an outer/valence electron and the reduction due to shielding by inner electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark when the electron and shielding idea are correctly connected.

modelAnswer: Effective nuclear charge is the net positive charge experienced by an outermost electron after the shielding effect of inner electrons is taken into account.

items.followUp: How does hydrogen bonding affect the boiling point of water?

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding creates stronger attractions between molecules, requiring more energy to separate them.
rubric.description: States that hydrogen bonding raises the boiling point of a substance.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect on boiling point.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding also influences other physical properties by strengthening intermolecular attraction.
rubric.description: Names another physical property affected by hydrogen bonding, such as surface tension, viscosity or melting point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid additional property.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding strengthens the attraction between molecules, so more energy is needed to separate them and the boiling point is higher.
It also affects physical properties such as surface tension, viscosity and melting point.

items.followUp: How many covalent bonds are present in an oxygen molecule, and what is their type?

rubric.why: Each nitrogen atom shares three electron pairs with the other nitrogen atom.
rubric.description: Identifies the N₂ bond as a triple covalent bond.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a triple bond.

rubric.why: A triple bond consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds.
rubric.description: States the composition of the triple bond as one sigma and two pi bonds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct bond composition.

modelAnswer: A nitrogen molecule (N₂) contains a triple covalent bond between its two nitrogen atoms.
This triple bond consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds.
